A companion deep-dive to the main MABench evaluation,
[*Machines Improving Agents*](../the-benchmark/index.qmd). MABench hands an
optimization method a copy of a seed agent and a metered budget; the method
checkpoints whatever it thinks is its best, and only those checkpoints are
scored — later, on a **sealed** test split it never sees. Everything here is
the *frontier-worker slice* of the grid: worker `gpt-5.6-luna`, meta model
`gpt-5.6-sol` or `claude-opus-5`, with every lift measured as Δ over the
seed's own genesis. Keep the noise floor in mind — one full eval's
run-to-run spread is a few points, so a lift smaller than that is
indistinguishable from re-scoring an unchanged agent (the
[main post](../the-benchmark/index.qmd) reports the exact floor).

Of the four methods, AdaEvolve is the one we have taken fully apart — its
checkpoints keep every program it wrote alongside the exact prompt its
proposer saw, so a run can be reconstructed edit by edit. AdaEvolve ran only
on the minimal-seed tier here, and this post explains a fact the
[main evaluation](../the-benchmark/index.qmd)'s tables leave standing: across
the frontier-worker grid AdaEvolve posts the largest per-method mean, yet
almost all of that mean is one benchmark.<!-- TODO: figure — AdaEvolve
best-so-far curve vs a permutation null, with the iteration-1/iteration-3
duplicate marked -->

**What kind of edit pays — the question MABench poses of every method — has
a clean answer: genuine structure, not prompt strings hiding in code.**
AdaEvolve's winning τ² program grew from 12 to 156 lines by *deleting* the
hand-written prompt prose and replacing it with runtime machinery — a
regex-built "high-risk clause index" over whatever policy the task passes in,
and a sanitized task capsule whose blocklist explicitly refuses the oracle
fields (`expected_actions`, `reward`, `initial_state`). Not one
instance-specific string anywhere. Its CharXiv winner is the same shape: a
draft pass plus a skeptical second "auditor" pass over six overlapping crops.
So AdaEvolve is not a prompt optimizer with a compiler's reach — when it
works, it is editing control flow.

**The catch is that the signal it climbs is noisier than the steps it
takes.** AdaEvolve keeps only its current best program as the parent to beat
— a champion hill-climb (the parent is the global best in 95–98% of
iterations). On GPQA and CharXiv the accepted improvements are almost all
worth a single train task, while one evaluation of the training split
carries a standard error of roughly two to three tasks — so on those two
benchmarks the hill it climbs is hard to separate from the order statistic
of its own eval noise. The sharpest illustration: on GPQA the run's one
genuine change landed at iteration 1 — a prompt rewrite worth about +2–3
test points — and the "accepted improvement" three iterations later, scoring
0.954, is byte-identical (same content hash) to that iteration-1 program. It
was a single lucky evaluation of code whose five re-scores span 0.892–0.954,
and that noise peak then stood as the unbeatable parent for 290 of the
remaining 297 iterations. The proposer never learned otherwise, because it
is fed scalars only: across all 353 stored proposer prompts the "previous
attempts" field reads *"No previous attempts yet."* every time, and not one
response references a task id. Selection pressure, not information, is the
whole feedback loop.

**Where it does work, the direction comes from the proposer's prior, not the
scores.** τ² is the exception, and it is diagnostic. There the run is
genuinely directed — monotone dev gains (0.576 → 0.739), compounding
structural rewrites, and records that arrive *later* than any reshuffle of
the same scores (a real upward trend, not noise-peak capture). But the
direction did not come from the scores, which are the same bare scalar as
everywhere else — it came from what the proposer thought to try.
`gpt-5.6-sol` proposed reading the task metadata in 35 of 74 proposals on
that seed and found the capsule; `claude-opus-5` proposed it 3 times in 65
on the identical seed and never did. That single difference in prior is the
largest outcome swing in the sweep — and the τ² program is also the most
portable artifact in the grid, gaining +6.1 under luna and **+13.3** when
that same frozen program is re-scored with the worker swapped down to
`haiku-4.5`: the weaker worker benefits *more* from a scaffold it was never
tuned against.

**And removing dev selection does not remove the winner's curse — it
relocates it to train.** AdaEvolve is the one method that never selects on
dev at all; it ranks candidates on train fitness only, which makes it the
clean test of whether the dev→test gap is really about the dev split. It is
not. On CharXiv the winner is impeccably structural — the crop-and-audit
pipeline, zero memorized content — and still lost 4.0 points on the sealed
test: its train fitness had climbed from 0.794 to a nominal 0.853 through
accepted steps at iterations 1–3, 15, 27 and 62, but re-scoring that same
champion at the end of the run returned 0.809. Most of the climb was eval
noise the search had banked as progress. Whatever split supplies the
selection signal absorbs the overfit — dev for the dev-selecting methods,
train for this one.

The one-line read: AdaEvolve makes the most generalizable edits in the
sweep when a structural idea happens to live in its proposer's prior, and
spends most of the rest of its budget climbing noise. Its expected value is
dominated by run-to-run variance — the same method produced the grid's
largest single transfer and a 297-iteration dead stall.
